title: Abba (Mark 14:32–42)
hook: in Gethsemane he calls God Abba, Father, and asks for the cup to pass

segments.voice: Yesterday, skandalon, Peter said, not me. Your line was not I said Peter. Did you catch yourself being too sure? Day two hundred twenty-one.

After supper they go out to the Mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. Tradition says the name means oil press, the place where olives are crushed. Jesus tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, and takes Peter, James and John a little further. And Mark says something about Jesus we haven't heard before: he began to be deeply distressed and troubled. He says to them, in the King James Bible: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." Then he goes a little further on alone, and falls on the ground. Not kneeling, composed. On the ground. And the first word out of his mouth is today's word.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED GETHSEMANE.` → `SORROWFUL UNTO DEATH.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is an Aramaic word. Mark keeps it, then translates it for his Greek readers: Father. You may have heard that abba means daddy. Mark doesn't say that; he gives it simply as Father. And Paul, writing in Greek to grown men and women, keeps the word too: they cry Abba, Father. So whatever else it is, it isn't baby talk. It's family talk, said by a son in the dark. And listen to the whole prayer. All things are possible to you: the same words he gave the father of the boy, and the disciples at the needle's eye. Take away this cup: Isaiah speaks of a cup of trembling. And then the turn: not what I will, but what you will. He asks honestly for what he wants, and then hands it over. Then he comes back, and they're asleep. "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?" Watch, the word from a few days ago. "The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak." He goes and prays the same words again. Comes back: asleep. A third time. Then: it is enough. The hour has come. Rise up, let's go. Many Christians see here both how human Jesus was, and how he trusted. In the dark, face down, he still says Abba.
screen: `ABBA: MARK SAYS FATHER.` · `NOT DADDY, BUT NOT DISTANT.` · `TAKE THIS CUP, YET THY WILL.` · `COULDEST NOT THOU WATCH ONE HOUR?` · then, large: `NOT WHAT I WILL, BUT WHAT THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak as a child to a parent. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you'd say if you could be completely honest with someone who loves you. What do you want taken away? What are you afraid of? If you pray, you can speak to God the way Jesus did: Abba, Father. Say what you want, plainly. And then, only if you can, add his next words: nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt. If you don't pray, just let yourself be honest, like a child would be. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word a child uses at home. Jesus's first word in Gethsemane.
Your line: abba, father. Today, when something feels too heavy, say what you want honestly, and then see if you can let it go. Day two hundred twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 221 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KISS AND THE LINEN.`

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Jesus's words "not what I will, but what thou wilt" in times of struggle, and some churches keep a watch of prayer late on Maundy Thursday night in memory of Gethsemane.

original.note: Aramaic for father, written in Greek letters in Mark 14:36, then translated: ho patēr.

trapdoor: what you thought: abba means daddy.
what it means: the family word for father, prayed in Gethsemane: close, trusting, and still respectful.
what a scholar hears: an Aramaic word Mark kept, which Paul keeps too (Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). Mark translates it ho patēr, Father.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): "Olive grove" (from John, not Mark) and "the name likely means oil press" recast; oil press now "tradition says". The abba paragraph no longer rests on unsourced scholarship ("scholars later pointed out", "the everyday language Jesus spoke", "early Christians loved the word"); it now stays with what Mark and Paul show. Hook line telling the listener "you know this place" replaced. "Christians of every church" softened. Cup image tied to Isaiah 51:17 (now cited). Screen heads, match, myth and trapdoor aligned.
Gethsemane as 'oil press' (Aramaic gat shemanin): the likely etymology; script says 'likely'.
'Abba is not daddy': Joachim Jeremias popularized the intimate 'daddy' reading; James Barr (1988) and others challenged it. Stated as 'scholars later pointed out'. Confirm.
The cup as a prophetic image of suffering/judgment (e.g. Isaiah 51:17). Confirm phrasing.
Review uses 'not I said Peter' without the comma so the validator's neighbor check matches; the carry itself is exact on screen.
Practice quotes a real scripture line (14:36) as an optional prayer.
